title: Privilege Escalation
summary: Privilege Escalation is the tactic covering the steps an adversary takes to move from a foothold with ordinary user rights to something far more powerful, whether that means local administrator on one host, domain-wide control, or an equivalent role in a cloud tenant. Behaviours include exploiting misconfigured services and file permissions, abusing elevation control mechanisms such as user account control bypasses, injecting code into higher-privileged processes, stealing tokens, taking advantage of overly broad sudo or role assignments, and exploiting vulnerable kernel or driver components. The defender's view differs sharply by platform. On endpoints, escalation generates process access events, token manipulation, unusual child processes of privileged services, new service or driver installation, and integrity-level changes. In identity and cloud environments it appears as role assumption, policy attachment, group membership change, or a sudden expansion of what a principal can do. This is one of the hardest tactics to detect in isolation because legitimate administration produces the same primitives, and because many escalations are simply the use of permissions that were granted too generously rather than an obvious exploitation event. Meaningful detection requires modelling what each principal should be able to do, alerting on capability changes rather than individual actions, and correlating an escalation with whatever access it enabled next, such as credential dumping or lateral movement.
objectives: Map the privilege escalation paths that matter most on Windows, Linux, and major cloud platforms, and explain how each is normally abused.
Explain what process access, token, and integrity-level telemetry reveals about escalation attempts and where it is blind.
Model expected privileges per principal so that capability expansion is detectable without relying on signature-style rules.
Correlate an escalation event with the credential access or lateral movement that follows it to establish intent and impact.
Identify the configuration weaknesses, excessive permissions, and unpatched components that make escalation possible in the first place.
Prioritise hardening actions by realistic exploitability rather than by scanner severity alone.
